record.ear: Fair and cold. High 40. Low 29. St. Patrick's parade at 1 p.m., the feast falling on Sunday.

lead.headline: Ice and coal carried by hand to 1,312 doors on the stoppage's first day
lead.deck: No horse beneath the elevated from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m.; 41 hand-carts and about 300 buckets; two ice men treated for strains; the Hallett's Point company asks its drivers to reconsider
lead.body: No horse passed beneath the elevated on Roosevelt Avenue between 6 a.m. and 7 p.m. yesterday, the first day of the carters' stoppage. Mr. Dennis Rafferty, secretary of the carters' association, stated that ice and coal were carried by hand from the corners to 1,312 doors, with 41 hand-carts and 'about 300 buckets.' Two ice men were treated at St. John's Hospital for strains. The Transit Commission had nothing to add. The Hallett's Point Ice Company has asked its drivers to reconsider by Monday.

columns.headline: Week's count: Exchange logs 3,906 night calls concerning a tone
columns.body: The Queens Exchange logged 3,906 calls in the seven nights to Thursday asking whether a tone heard between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. was 'on the line or in the house,' Superintendent Wilfred Arne states, against 1,210 in early March. The Exchange 'cannot say.'

columns.headline: St. Patrick's parade on Fifth Avenue today; Society to record at the same spot
columns.body: The St. Patrick's Day parade will march up Fifth Avenue at 1 p.m. today, the feast falling on Sunday. The Phonautograph Society of Queens will record it from the steps of the Public Library, 'at the spot where it was recorded last year,' Mr. Cyril Abbot states.

columns.headline: Crews of the Byrd ships to be heard from Dunedin harbour tomorrow at 9 p.m.
columns.body: The crews of the City of New York and the Eleanor Bolling will be heard by wire from Dunedin harbour tomorrow at 9 p.m. Little America, which reported nightly through March 14, has not been heard since, the Navy's station at Bay Shore states.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The drivers of the Hallett's Point Ice Company voted at 9 p.m. to remain out with the association.

speaker.ear: Fair and cold. High 40. The Irish march today. The El would march too, if asked nicely.

lead.headline: Carters hang up on the El, and the ice gets through by hand
lead.deck: Thirteen hundred doors served from the corners; two ice men strained; Hallett's Point thinks it over and thinks better of it; the horses are reported rested and smug
lead.body: For the whole of Friday, from six in the morning till seven at night, the El ran over Roosevelt Avenue and not one horse ran under it. Forty-one hand-carts and three hundred buckets carried the ice and coal from the corners to thirteen hundred doors. Two ice men went to St. John's with their backs. The Transit Commission had nothing to add, and added it twice. The horses spent the day in the stables, eating, and are said never to have looked better.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Is the Hum louder, or is it me?'
columns.body: Sir, the Exchange took three thousand nine hundred and six calls this week asking the same thing, all between one and four in the morning. The operator cannot say. She can say that the Hum is the only caller in Queens that never asks for anybody, and never hangs up.

columns.headline: Society will record the pipes again, to see which year was in better tune
columns.body: Mr. Abbot will set up on the Library steps at one today, where he set up last year, and take the parade down again so that 1978 may compare the two. He says the comparison is scientific. We say last year it rained, so the comparison is umbrellas.

columns.headline: Byrd's camp goes off the air, and Bay Shore keeps the receiver warm
columns.body: Little America has not been heard since Thursday night, when it said thirty-three below and all well. The Navy says the camp is probably saving its batteries. The camp's batteries are the size of a coal cellar. We are keeping a lamp in the window anyway.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Hallett's Point's drivers voted tonight to stay out. Their horses voted with their feet, which were up.

editorial.headline: Ash dump burns; she carries children; we smell publicity
editorial.body: When the Flushing ash dumps caught fire on Tuesday and the smoke rolled over the shanties of Corona, a woman in black was seen going in and out of the smoke along the roofs of the shanties, bringing out children by twos, until the last was counted and she was gone. Firemen confirm nine children. Mothers confirm nine. The Speaker confirms that this was, in its way, a fine thing to do, and adds that a fine thing done in a mask is a fine thing done for the newspapers. Real heroes give their names. We gave ours, which is how she knew where to send the bill for nine children's shoes, which arrived Thursday, paid.

record.ear: Fair. High 45. Low 33. St. Patrick's Day.

lead.headline: Parade recorded at the Library steps; cheering 9 seconds shorter than 1928
lead.deck: The 69th Regiment led at 1:09 p.m.; pipes 'somewhat louder,' drums unchanged; the two years' records played on the steps at 5 p.m. to about 400
lead.body: The St. Patrick's Day parade passed the steps of the Public Library on Fifth Avenue from 1:09 p.m. to 4:47 p.m. yesterday, the 69th Regiment leading, and was recorded by the Phonautograph Society of Queens at the spot where it was recorded last year. Mr. Cyril Abbot stated that the cheering at the reviewing stand ran 9 seconds shorter than in 1928, and the pipes 'somewhat louder.' At 5 p.m. the two records were played on the steps to about 400.

columns.headline: Little America not heard for three nights; Bay Shore listens from 8 p.m.
columns.body: The Navy's receiving station at Bay Shore has not heard the Little America camp since 10:40 p.m. Thursday, its operator states. The station listens nightly from 8 p.m. to 2 a.m. The ships at Dunedin report 'no word from the ice either.'

columns.headline: Carters' stoppage holds on its second day; Sunday deliveries suspended
columns.body: No horse passed beneath the elevated on Roosevelt Avenue yesterday, the stoppage's second day, Mr. Dennis Rafferty states, the Hallett's Point drivers having voted on Friday night to remain out. Sunday deliveries are suspended as usual. The Transit Commission meets on Tuesday.

columns.headline: Queens Light & Power attributes night complaints to 'the thaw in the ground'
columns.body: A spokesman for Queens Light & Power stated yesterday that the night complaints logged at the Exchange are 'consistent with the thaw,' frost leaving the ground being 'a noisy process.' The company denies any tone. Dr. Emil Rastin of Columbia stated that he had 'not measured the frost.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The crews of the Byrd ships will be heard from Dunedin at 9 p.m.; the Record's window opens at 8:30.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 45. Wear the green. The Hum is wearing whatever it likes.

lead.headline: The parade marches past twice, and the cheering falls short of the record
lead.deck: Mr. Abbot plays 1928 and 1929 back to back on the Library steps; the pipes win; the crowd, hearing itself last year, cheers last year all over again
lead.body: Mr. Abbot of the Phonautograph Society stood on the Library steps at five yesterday and played the crowd last year's parade, then this year's. This year's cheering was nine seconds shorter. The pipes were louder, the drums were the drums, and last year it rained. When the 1928 record reached the 69th Regiment, the crowd of four hundred cheered it, which Mr. Abbot says spoils the experiment, because next year he will have to compare it with that.

columns.headline: Light company thaws out a new excuse, and the Hum stays on the line
columns.body: Queens Light & Power says the tone that wakes three thousand callers a week is the frost leaving the ground, which it calls a noisy process. Dr. Rastin says he has never measured frost. We have listened to our own yard all night. It is a lawn.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? A Maspeth reader has the word, and won't send it down the wire
columns.body: A reader in Maspeth writes that she knows the last word WORS said to the girl on 61st Street, and will tell it to Mr. Pike in person, but not to the Speaker, nor the operator. Mr. Pike says he does not need telling. Pin ninety-six stays red.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Can I ring my mother in Cork?'
columns.body: Sir, the Exchange can put you through to the cable, and the cable will take you as far as Valentia, and Valentia knows a man in Cork. It will cost eleven dollars for three minutes. Your mother will spend all three asking what it costs.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Byrd ships' crews came through from Dunedin tonight and asked for news of the camp. So did we.

lead.headline: Byrd ships' crews heard from Dunedin; Little America silent since Thursday
lead.deck: Twenty-two minutes from the harbour from 9:04 p.m.; Captain Melville: the ships 'well and refitting'; about 600 at the Record's window
lead.body: The crews of the City of New York and the Eleanor Bolling were heard from Dunedin harbour at 9:04 p.m. yesterday for 22 minutes, and played in the Record's window to about 600. Captain Frederick Melville of the City of New York stated that the ships 'are well and refitting.' Asked by the Navy's operator for word from Little America, he said there had been 'none since Thursday.' The Navy states that the camp is believed to be conserving power for the winter.

columns.headline: Yankees beat the Braves 7 to 4 at St. Petersburg; swings played at supper
columns.body: The Yankees beat the Boston Braves 7 to 4 at St. Petersburg on Saturday, the club's operator carrying the game north by wire. Mr. Tony Lazzeri had two hits. Manager Miller Huggins stated that the players' recorded swings 'are being played back to them at supper.'

columns.headline: Appellate Division hears Mr. Gorman's appeal on the Riverhead seal at 10 a.m.
columns.body: The Appellate Division at Brooklyn hears at 10 a.m. today the appeal of Mr. Francis Gorman against the Board of Elections' seal on 11 seconds of its Riverhead record. Counsel for each side is allowed 40 minutes. The warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti, lineman, remains outstanding.

columns.headline: Commissioner Lacey rules at 2 p.m. on the instrument for the Astoria works
columns.body: Commissioner Maurice Lacey of the Public Service Commission will rule at 2 p.m. today on the objection of Queens Light & Power to Dr. Emil Rastin's meter being carried into its Astoria works by Mr. Aldous Venn on March 28. The company has submitted a meter of its own make.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The carters' association states that the stoppage beneath the elevated continues from 6 a.m. today.

speaker.ear: Cloudy. High 47. Monday. The ice camp is quiet. So is the ice.

lead.headline: Byrd's ships ring home from Dunedin, and the ice camp still isn't picking up
lead.deck: Twenty-two minutes from the harbour; Captain Melville says the ships are well; asked after Little America, he says what we say: nothing since Thursday
lead.body: The ships came through at four minutes past nine last night, twenty-two minutes of sailors saying hello to Brooklyn, Bayonne and a girl in Astoria named Vera. Six hundred people stood outside the Record's window to hear it, and we stood with them, because our window has no wire. Then Bay Shore asked the captain for word from the ice. He said there had been none since Thursday. The crowd went home quieter. Vera, we are told, went home pleased.

columns.headline: Yankees play it back at supper, and Lazzeri loses his appetite
columns.body: Seven to four over the Braves at St. Petersburg on Saturday, and Mr. Huggins has the day's swings played back at supper. Mr. Lazzeri, two hits, says he cannot eat while hearing himself pop up. Mr. Huggins says that is the idea.

columns.headline: Eleven seconds of dead air go to appeal, and Gorman wants them live
columns.body: Today in Brooklyn Mr. Gorman's counsel gets forty minutes to argue that eleven sealed seconds of the Riverhead count should be heard. The Board gets forty to argue they should not. That is eighty minutes about eleven seconds. Mr. Marchetti, wanted, is not expected to attend.

columns.headline: Lacey decides which meter goes in, and the company wants its own reading
columns.body: Commissioner Lacey decides at two this afternoon whether Mr. Venn takes Dr. Rastin's meter into the Astoria works or the light company's, which the company has kindly lent. Dr. Rastin says he is happy for both to go. The company has not said whether it is.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The carters are still out. The horses have asked that the stoppage be made permanent.

lead.headline: Commissioner Lacey rules both meters shall be carried into the Astoria works
lead.deck: Dr. Rastin's instrument and the company's 'side by side'; each to be read aloud by the other party; readings sealed until April 2; Mr. Tisch accepts 'under protest'
lead.body: Commissioner Maurice Lacey ruled at 2:20 p.m. yesterday that Mr. Aldous Venn shall carry into the Astoria works of Queens Light & Power on March 28 both the meter of Dr. Emil Rastin and the meter submitted by the company, 'side by side,' each to be read aloud by the other party's representative, and the readings recorded and sealed until the Commission's hearing of April 2. Mr. Roland Tisch, for the company, accepted the ruling 'under protest.' Dr. Rastin stated that he was 'content.'

columns.headline: Appellate Division reserves decision on the Riverhead seal after 80 minutes
columns.body: The Appellate Division reserved decision yesterday on Mr. Francis Gorman's appeal against the Board of Elections' seal on 11 seconds of its Riverhead record. Justice Ward Hollins asked counsel for the Board whether the Board 'had itself heard the 11 seconds.' Counsel said it had not.

columns.headline: Transit Commission to consider the carters' letter at 11 a.m. today
columns.body: The Transit Commission will take up at 11 a.m. today the carters' association's letter of February 22, the stoppage beneath the elevated having entered its fifth day. Ice companies report delivery costs 'about doubled.' No horse has fallen on Roosevelt Avenue since March 11.

columns.headline: Levee station at Cairo reports the Ohio at 48.6 feet and rising
columns.body: The levee station at Cairo, Illinois, reported by wire at 6 p.m. yesterday that the Ohio stood at 48.6 feet and rising, and that its house system 'hears the water on the levee face' at night. The Weather Bureau forecasts a crest of about 50 feet by Thursday.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Queens Exchange received 702 calls concerning a night tone between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. yesterday.

speaker.ear: Cloudy. High 49. The Ohio is rising. The Hum is rising. The Speaker is rising to the occasion.

lead.headline: Both meters go into the works, and Lacey puts both sides on one wavelength
lead.deck: Rastin's meter and the company's to sit side by side on the 28th; each read aloud by the enemy; the lot sealed till April; Mr. Tisch accepts under protest, his favourite key
lead.body: Commissioner Lacey has done what any mother does with two boys and one cake. On the twenty-eighth Mr. Venn will carry two meters into the Astoria works, Dr. Rastin's and the company's, and set them down side by side. The company's man will read Dr. Rastin's aloud. Dr. Rastin's man will read the company's. The whole performance will be recorded and sealed until the second of April. Mr. Tisch accepted under protest. Dr. Rastin said he was content. Duke of 31st Street was not consulted.

columns.headline: The Ohio climbs the levee, and the levee calls it in
columns.body: At Cairo, Illinois, the levee station's house system hears the Ohio on the levee face all night, and wires the height every six hours. Last night it was forty-eight feet six. The levee says it is holding. It is the first levee in history to say so personally.

columns.headline: Gorman's eleven seconds stay on hold while the bench thinks it over
columns.body: Eighty minutes of argument in Brooklyn yesterday, and the court reserved decision. One justice asked the Board's counsel whether the Board had ever heard its own eleven seconds. Counsel said no. The justice said nothing for about eleven seconds. Nobody recorded it.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: Jackson Heights tunes in to the small hours
columns.body: Darlings, a Jackson Heights hostess kept awake by the tone at three in the morning now gives a little supper at that hour, so that her guests may be kept awake together. The tone attends. It is the only guest who never needs its coat fetched.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Seven hundred and two subscribers rang the Exchange about the Hum last night. The light company blames the thaw. The thaw is not taking calls.

record.ear: Fair. High 52. Low 39. Spring begins tomorrow.

lead.headline: Transit Commission orders sanding beneath the elevated for a 30-day trial
lead.deck: Order made at 12:40 p.m. after a 90-minute meeting; drip trays between 74th and 82nd Streets; no reference to the association's letter; carters to vote tonight
lead.body: The Transit Commission ordered at 12:40 p.m. yesterday that Roosevelt Avenue beneath the elevated, from Queensboro Plaza to 103rd Street, be sanded each morning by 5 a.m. for a trial of 30 days, and that drip trays be fitted to the structure between 74th and 82nd Streets. The order makes no reference to the carters' association's letter. Mr. Dennis Rafferty stated that members would vote at Woodside Hall at 8 p.m. today, and that the order 'is what we asked for on February 22.'

columns.headline: Senate committee receives three amendments to the Listening Act
columns.body: Senator Edmund Harlan's Judiciary Committee received yesterday three amendments to the Listening Act, to be heard March 27: Senator Rufus Keel's, barring records of bedrooms without the consent 'of every party to the room'; Senator Ames Whitlock's, licensing insurance adjusters' acoustic work; and Senator Daniel Fogarty's, exempting places of confession.

columns.headline: Dr. Strand to sing the 23rd bar to Aberystwyth by cable tomorrow at 2 p.m.
columns.body: Dr. Matthias Strand of Union Seminary will sing the 23rd bar of the carol heard on WORS 1610 to the National Library of Wales by cable at 2 p.m. tomorrow, the Library having accepted his offer. The call is booked for six minutes from the Broad Street cable office.

columns.headline: Valves at 82 cents the sleeve, three cents below December; eggs 51
columns.body: The sleeve of receiving valves sold at 82 cents at the Vantry Arcade's hardware counter yesterday, three cents below last December's price, Mr. Jacob Fass reports. Eggs were 51 cents. Mr. Fass states that 'nobody is buying ahead now,' and that he holds 300 sleeves in the cellar.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The levee station at Cairo, Illinois, reported the Ohio at 49.3 feet at midnight.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 52. Spring arrives tomorrow. The Commission got there early, for once.

lead.headline: The Commission finally picks up, and Roosevelt Avenue gets its sand
lead.deck: Sand by five every morning for thirty days; drip trays at 74th; no mention of the letter; the carters vote tonight and the horses are said to be packing
lead.body: Twenty-six days after the carters wrote, and five days after they stopped, the Transit Commission has ordered Roosevelt Avenue sanded under the El by five every morning for thirty days, with drip trays fitted between 74th and 82nd Streets. The order does not mention the carters, their letter or the twenty-four horses. Mr. Rafferty says it is what they asked for in February, word for word, and the members vote tonight. Biddy of the Corona Ice Company has not been told, in case it goes to her head.

columns.headline: Albany adds a priest's clause, and the Act goes to confession
columns.body: Three amendments are in for the Senate committee on the twenty-seventh. Senator Keel's keeps the bedroom off the record without everybody's say-so. Senator Whitlock's licenses insurance men who listen to pipes. Senator Fogarty's keeps the confessional out altogether. Father, forgive them. They are only amending.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Can you put me through to Wales?'
columns.body: Madam, the Exchange can, and tomorrow at two it is putting Dr. Strand through, for six minutes, so that he may sing one bar of the WORS carol to a library. The operator will be listening. She asks that nobody else ring Wales tomorrow, in case it is catching.

columns.headline: Valves drop to eighty-two, and Mr. Fass has three hundred sleeves on hold
columns.body: Eighty-two cents the sleeve yesterday, cheaper than December. Mr. Fass of the Arcade counter says nobody buys ahead now, and he has three hundred sleeves in his cellar, bought in January at a dollar thirty. He is keeping them for sentimental reasons. Eggs are fifty-one.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Ohio at Cairo is forty-nine feet three and climbing. The levee is still talking. It says it is fine.

record.ear: Fair and milder. High 55. Low 40. The first day of spring.

lead.headline: Carters vote 288 to 17 to resume deliveries beneath the elevated Friday
lead.deck: Woodside Hall meeting from 8 p.m. to 9:25 p.m.; the stoppage to end on its seventh day; an association member to inspect the sand each morning; cost put at 4,100 dollars
lead.body: The Long Island City carters' association voted at Woodside Hall at 9:20 p.m. yesterday, by 288 votes to 17, to resume deliveries of ice and coal beneath the elevated on Roosevelt Avenue from 6 a.m. tomorrow, the Transit Commission having ordered the roadway sanded each morning for 30 days. Mr. Dennis Rafferty stated that a member will 'walk the avenue at 5 a.m. each day and look at the sand.' The ice companies estimate its cost at 4,100 dollars.

columns.headline: Little America not heard for seven nights; Navy 'not concerned'
columns.body: The Navy's station at Bay Shore stated at 2 a.m. today that Little America has not been heard for seven nights. A Navy spokesman stated that the Department is 'not concerned,' the camp having 'ample stores and dogs.' The Record's window will play any message received.

columns.headline: Unsigned lease renewals found beneath the doors of the Arcade's eleven shops
columns.body: Each of the eleven tenants of the Vantry Arcade found beneath the shop door yesterday morning a renewal of lease for one year from May 1 at the present rent, typed, in the name of Signal Ground Rents Inc., and unsigned. The post office states that no postman delivered them.

columns.headline: Dr. Strand sings to the National Library of Wales at 2 p.m. today
columns.body: Dr. Matthias Strand will sing at 2 p.m. today, from the cable office on Broad Street, the 23rd bar of the carol heard on WORS 1610 to the National Library of Wales, which will record the call. Dr. Strand states that the bar 'takes about four seconds.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The levee station at Cairo, Illinois, reported the Ohio at 49.8 feet at 1 a.m., rising more slowly.

speaker.ear: Spring. High 55. The Arcade got its leases. Nobody signed them. Spring is like that.

lead.headline: Signal Ground Rents sends its regards, and forgets to sign off
lead.deck: Eleven renewals under eleven doors at the Arcade; a year from May at the same rent; no postman, no stamp, no name, and the telephone still ringing out
lead.body: Yesterday morning each of the eleven shops in the Vantry Arcade found a lease under its door: a year from the first of May, same rent, typed neatly in the name of Signal Ground Rents Inc., which has never once answered its telephone. Nobody had signed them. The post office says no postman brought them. The luncheonette read his twice and calls it the best offer he ever had from a landlord who does not exist. The toy shop has put hers in the drawer with the dolls.

columns.headline: The carters vote to get back on the line
columns.body: Two hundred and eighty-eight to seventeen in Woodside last night: the carters go back under the El at six tomorrow morning, on the sand. One of them will walk the avenue at five each day to look at it. The horses say the week was worth it.

columns.headline: The Ohio crests at Cairo, and the levee keeps up its end of the conversation
columns.body: The Ohio stopped climbing at Cairo late today, at fifty feet and a bit, and the levee station wired it in, as it has every six hours all week. The levee has held. Several readers have asked whether they might hear its record of itself. The levee is in Illinois.

columns.headline: Dr. Strand sings bar twenty-three to Wales, and the cable carries a tune
columns.body: At two this afternoon Dr. Strand stood in the cable office on Broad Street and sang the WORS carol to Aberystwyth, six minutes' money for four seconds that matter. The Library recorded it. He came out and said it had gone through. We shall see what Wales says.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The toy shop's lease is in the drawer with the dolls. The drawer was facing the door this morning.

lead.headline: Library of Wales records 22 bars of Dr. Strand's call; the 23rd 'not received'
lead.deck: Call of six minutes from Broad Street at 2 p.m.; in the place of the bar 'the singer's breath and the line's own noise'; the cable office operator states she heard it sung
lead.body: The National Library of Wales cabled Dr. Matthias Strand at 9 p.m. yesterday that its record of his call from the Broad Street cable office at 2 p.m. contains the 22 bars of the carol heard on WORS 1610, which Dr. Strand sang as a lead-in, and in the place of the 23rd bar 'the singer's breath and the line's own noise, about four seconds.' The operator at the Broad Street office states that she heard the bar sung. Dr. Strand will try again on Monday.

columns.headline: Tin in Mr. Marchetti's bag a Portland sardine sold by three Corona grocers
columns.body: The District Attorney's office stated yesterday that the empty sardine tin found in the tool bag of Mr. Joseph Marchetti is a Portland, Maine, packing 'sold at three grocers in Corona and none elsewhere in Queens.' No parcel has come to the Exchange's cat since February 22.

columns.headline: Sand laid beneath the elevated from 3:40 a.m.; carters to resume at 6 a.m.
columns.body: Transit Commission crews were to sand Roosevelt Avenue beneath the elevated from 3:40 a.m. today, an association member walking behind them, and the carters' first wagons to pass beneath the structure at 6 a.m., Mr. Dennis Rafferty states. The stoppage ends on its seventh day.

columns.headline: Queens parishes order about 40,000 palms for Sunday, Chancery states
columns.body: Queens parishes have ordered about 40,000 palms for Palm Sunday, the Chancery states. The Passion will be read at High Mass and carried by telephone from nine parishes for the housebound, subscribers ringing before 9:30 a.m. Last Friday's Stations were heard by about 3,800 subscribers.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Corona Ice Company states that its grey mare Biddy will take the first wagon beneath the elevated at 6 a.m.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 50. Friday. Sardines for some.

lead.headline: D.A. traces the tin to Corona, and Party Line holds for a fourth Friday
lead.deck: Marchetti's empty tin is a Portland sardine sold at three Corona grocers and nowhere else; four o'clock comes and goes at the parcel window; the cat sits on, unanswered
lead.body: The empty tin in Mr. Marchetti's tool bag is a Portland, Maine, sardine sold at three grocers in Corona and nowhere else in Queens, the District Attorney says. The tins that came to Party Line every Friday until February were postmarked Corona. This afternoon was the fourth Friday without one. Party Line sat at the parcel window from four until six, then went back to the warm end of the board where the Corona calls come in. The warrant is still out. So is the lineman.

columns.headline: Biddy leads them back under the El, and Roosevelt Avenue rings with hooves
columns.body: At one minute past six this morning Biddy of the Corona Ice Company took the first wagon back under the elevated on fresh sand, an association man walking ahead with a lantern. Two hundred wagons followed by noon. The El dripped on every one of them. Nobody slipped.

columns.headline: Wales gets twenty-two bars and a breath, and the last one misses its connection
columns.body: Dr. Strand sang the WORS carol to Aberystwyth yesterday, twenty-two bars and then the one that will not go on paper. Wales says it got the twenty-two and then four seconds of breath. The Broad Street operator says she heard him sing it. He tries again on Monday.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Eleven nights of dead air, and the pins gather dust
columns.body: WORS has not been heard since the girl on 61st Street said goodnight to it eleven days ago. Mr. Pike's fourth launch has come in off North Beach for a coat of paint. The pins stand at ninety-six. Our office boy has been told he may dust them.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Two hundred wagons went under the El today. Not a horse down. The horses would like it known it was never them.

record.ear: Fair, rain by night. High 53. Low 41.

lead.headline: Week's count: 4,870 night calls on the tone; the company cites the thaw
lead.deck: Calls from every exchange district but Rockaway between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m.; 3,906 the week before; Dr. Rastin: the Astoria ground 'thawed in the first week of March'
lead.body: The Queens Exchange logged 4,870 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Thursday from subscribers reporting a tone, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states, against 3,906 the week before. Calls came from every exchange district but Rockaway. Queens Light & Power repeated that the night complaints are 'consistent with the thaw.' Dr. Emil Rastin stated that the ground at Astoria 'thawed in the first week of March, by the Weather Bureau's own figures.'

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society to seal its fifth copper case at Borough Hall April 13
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society of Queens will seal its fifth copper case in the vault at Borough Hall on April 13, Mr. Cyril Abbot states. Mrs. Ottoline Grieve has given notice that her fourth motion that record No. 23 be played will be moved April 12, 'the night before.'

columns.headline: Mr. Tully asks 20 minutes to oppose the bedroom amendment
columns.body: Mr. Ambrose Tully of the Real Estate Owners' Association asked Senator Harlan for 20 minutes of his hour on March 27 to oppose Senator Keel's bedroom amendment, which he said would 'make every lease a negotiation with the sleepers.' The Clerk's machine will be at the committee room door.

columns.headline: Brooklyn club beats the Braves 5 to 3 at Clearwater; bench told to keep quiet
columns.body: The Brooklyn club beat the Boston Braves 5 to 3 at Clearwater on Thursday. Manager Wilbert Robinson has ordered his bench 'to say nothing it would not want played back,' the club's wire carrying the dugout to Flatbush each afternoon.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Little America has not been heard for nine nights, the Navy's station at Bay Shore states.

speaker.ear: Fair, then rain. High 53. Palm Sunday tomorrow. Bring a palm and an umbrella.

lead.headline: Nine nights and not a peep from the ice, and Bay Shore stays tuned
lead.deck: The Navy says it is not concerned; the Speaker is; Little America has ample stores and dogs, and has mentioned neither since the fourteenth
lead.body: For nine nights the Navy's men at Bay Shore have sat up from eight till two with their earphones on, listening for Commander Byrd's camp at the bottom of the world, and for nine nights the camp has said nothing. The Navy says it is not concerned. The camp has stores for two years and ninety-odd dogs. We are concerned, on behalf of the dogs, the Commander and the Bay Shore men, who are concerned too, but are not allowed to say so.

columns.headline: Week's count: the Hum rings up four thousand eight hundred and seventy
columns.body: The Exchange took four thousand eight hundred and seventy calls about the night tone this week, up from three thousand nine hundred. The light company says the thaw. Dr. Rastin says the ground thawed three weeks ago. Rockaway alone made no calls. Rockaway is not saying why.

columns.headline: Uncle Robbie tells the bench to mind its tongue, and Flatbush tunes in anyway
columns.body: Mr. Robinson has told the Brooklyn bench at Clearwater to say nothing it would not want played back in Flatbush, the club's wire carrying the dugout north every afternoon. Flatbush reports that the bench has gone very quiet, and the language has improved by about eleven words.

columns.headline: Mrs. Grieve picks the night before the vault shuts, and Abbot faces the music
columns.body: The Society seals its fifth copper case on April thirteenth. Mrs. Grieve will move a fourth time, on the twelfth, that record No. 23 be played before it goes in. Mr. Abbot says it is not going in. Mrs. Grieve asks where, then, it is going.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Tully wants twenty minutes against the bedroom clause. The bedrooms want twenty minutes' peace.

editorial.headline: The horses strike and the borough walks
editorial.body: The carters' horse strike leaves the borough without coal and ice for a fourth day, and this paper blames the strikers, the horses and the weather in that order. Into the cold steps, of course, Lilith, who on Wednesday night made the coal yard owners of Newtown Creek a gift of their own price-fixing correspondence, read aloud on the wireless at midnight by a voice nobody can place, a soft, low, amused voice with a laugh in it like a match struck in the dark. The owners settled with the carters on Thursday. This paper did not enjoy the broadcast. We listened twice, purely to be certain of our ground.

lead.headline: New Madrid levee station hears water beneath the bank 40 minutes early
lead.deck: Report by wire at 3:10 a.m.; 600 men sandbagging; Mississippi at 41.2 feet; the Ohio's crest due Tuesday
lead.body: The levee station at New Madrid, Missouri, reported by wire at 3:10 a.m. yesterday that its house system had heard water moving beneath the levee 'some 40 minutes' before seepage was seen on the landward face, and that 600 men were placing sandbags. The Mississippi stood at 41.2 feet. The Weather Bureau states that the Ohio's crest, which passed Cairo on Thursday, will reach New Madrid by Tuesday. The levee stations of the Mississippi River Commission report every six hours.

columns.headline: Passion to be read in 61 Queens churches; nine parishes by telephone
columns.body: The Passion according to St. Matthew will be read at High Mass in 61 Queens churches today, and carried by telephone from nine parishes for the sick and housebound, subscribers ringing before 9:30 a.m., the Chancery states. About 40,000 palms have been distributed.

columns.headline: Yankees to break camp April 6 and play north through the Carolinas
columns.body: Manager Miller Huggins stated yesterday that the Yankees will break camp at St. Petersburg on April 6 and play their way north through the Carolinas, the club's operator carrying each game. The recorded swings will travel with the team, 'in two trunks.'

columns.headline: Greenpoint petitioners file 41 house records for the April 2 hearing
columns.body: Mr. Walter Szabo, secretary of the Greenpoint petitioners, filed with the Public Service Commission yesterday 41 house records made between midnight and 4 a.m. in the past fortnight, for the hearing of April 2. Mr. Szabo stated that the number 'is a coincidence.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Little America has not been heard for ten nights; the station at Bay Shore continues to listen from 8 p.m. to 2 a.m.

speaker.ear: Rain. High 50. Palm Sunday. The Speaker waves at you, damply.

lead.headline: The river calls ahead, and the levee picks up forty minutes early
lead.deck: New Madrid's house system hears water under the bank before any man sees it; six hundred sandbaggers on the job in time; the Mississippi at forty-one feet and the Ohio on its way
lead.body: At New Madrid, Missouri, the levee station's house system listens to the levee all night, because nobody else will. At ten past three yesterday morning it heard water moving under the bank, and forty minutes later a man with a lantern saw it come out the other side. By then six hundred men were already sandbagging. The levee held. The river is forty-one feet. The Ohio's crest arrives on Tuesday, and the levee says it is listening.

columns.headline: Greenpoint files forty-one records, and swears it isn't tuning the count
columns.body: Greenpoint has handed the Commission forty-one house records of the night tone for its hearing on April second. Mr. Szabo says the number is a coincidence. We counted twice and got forty-one both times. The Commission now has the records and the coincidence.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'May I hear Mass in bed?'
columns.body: Madam, nine parishes will carry the Passion by telephone this morning for the sick and housebound. The operator asks whether you are sick or housebound. If you are merely in bed, she suggests you get up. It is a long Gospel, and she has heard you snore.

columns.headline: Huggins ships his records north in two trunks, and the swing goes on tour
columns.body: The Yankees break camp on April sixth and play north through the Carolinas. Mr. Huggins is bringing the spring's recorded swings in two trunks. One trunk is the Babe's. The other is everybody else's. The trunks travel in a separate car, for safety.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Ten nights and no word from Byrd's camp. The Bay Shore men have asked for more coffee and fewer questions.

lead.headline: Ten of eleven Arcade tenants decline to sign the unsigned renewals
lead.deck: No address given for return; the news and cigar stand signs and puts the lease beneath its own door; on Sunday morning the lease is gone; the company rung three times
lead.body: Ten of the eleven tenants of the Vantry Arcade have decided not to sign the lease renewals found beneath their doors on Wednesday, Mr. Oscar Bliss of the luncheonette stated, the leases naming 'no address to which they could be returned.' The proprietor of the news and cigar stand signed his on Saturday and put it back beneath his own door. On Sunday morning it was gone. The telephone of Signal Ground Rents Inc. did not answer at 9 a.m., noon or 3 p.m.

columns.headline: Yankees beat the Braves 9 to 6; Brooklyn rained out at Clearwater
columns.body: The Yankees beat the Boston Braves 9 to 6 at St. Petersburg on Saturday before about 2,000, Mr. Tony Lazzeri hitting a home run. The Brooklyn club's game at Clearwater was abandoned for rain in the third inning, the club's operator reports.

columns.headline: Dr. Strand to sing the 23rd bar again at 2 p.m. by the Rockaway cable
columns.body: Dr. Matthias Strand will sing the 23rd bar of the WORS 1610 carol again at 2 p.m. today, by the cable from Rockaway, the Library having asked that he 'not sing the 22 first.' Dr. Strand states that the bar 'does not begin without them.'

columns.headline: Senate Judiciary Committee hears the Listening Act Wednesday at 2 p.m.
columns.body: Senator Edmund Harlan's Judiciary Committee will hear the Listening Act on Wednesday at 2 p.m., with the Keel, Whitlock and Fogarty amendments. Assemblyman Thomas Burkhardt will speak first. Msgr. Thomas Fennelly will speak for the Chancery. The Clerk's machine will be at the door.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Mississippi at New Madrid stood at 41.6 feet at midnight; the levee station reports 'holding.'

speaker.ear: Cloudy. High 54. Holy Week. The Speaker is giving up puns for Lent, from tomorrow.

lead.headline: The news stand signs, and his lease goes off the air by morning
lead.deck: Ten Arcade tenants won't sign for a landlord with no address; the eleventh signs, slips it under his own door, and on Sunday it is gone
lead.body: Ten of the eleven shops in the Vantry Arcade have looked at their unsigned leases from Signal Ground Rents and decided not to sign anything for a company with no address to send it back to. The eleventh, the news and cigar stand, signed his on Saturday and, not knowing where else to put it, slid it back under his own door. On Sunday morning it was gone. He has a year from May, he supposes. He sells this paper. We are keeping an eye on him for you.

columns.headline: Lazzeri hears his swing leave the park, then hears it again at supper
columns.body: Nine to six over the Braves on Saturday, Lazzeri with a home run, which Mr. Huggins had played back to him four times at supper. Brooklyn was rained out at Clearwater, which Uncle Robbie says is the best game they have played all spring.

columns.headline: Strand rings Wales again, and is told to skip the overture
columns.body: Wales has asked Dr. Strand to sing only the twenty-third bar this afternoon, not the twenty-two before it. Dr. Strand says the bar does not begin without them. He will try at two, by the Rockaway cable. The Broad Street operator has asked to listen in.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Two weeks off the air, and Woodside blames the goodnight
columns.body: WORS has not been heard since the girl on 61st Street said goodnight to it a fortnight ago Sunday. Woodside thinks it was offended. The girl thinks it went to sleep, as told. Pin ninety-six is still red. Mr. Pike's launch is back off North Beach, freshly painted.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Mississippi at New Madrid is forty-one feet six and the levee is holding. It says so every six hours, like a good boy.

lead.headline: Wales records breath where the 23rd bar was sung on the Rockaway call
lead.deck: Station operator and two Union Seminary witnesses in the booth heard the 23rd bar; Aberystwyth received breath and line noise again; the station's own record sent to the Radio Division
lead.body: The National Library of Wales cabled at 8:40 p.m. yesterday that its record of Dr. Matthias Strand's call from the Rockaway cable station at 2 p.m. contains his greeting, 'about four seconds of breath and line noise,' and his farewell. The station's operator and two members of the Union Seminary faculty, present in the booth, stated that they heard the 23rd bar sung. The station's own record of the call has been sent to Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division.

columns.headline: Navy asks the City of New York to listen for Little America from Dunedin
columns.body: The Navy Department asked the City of New York at Dunedin yesterday to listen nightly for Little America, not heard since March 14. The ship's operator reported at 11 p.m. 'nothing on the camp's wave but the ice.' The Navy states that it is 'not concerned.'

columns.headline: Tenebrae at St. Mary's on three evenings; the parish to record all three
columns.body: Tenebrae will be sung on the evenings of Wednesday, Thursday and Friday at St. Mary's, Long Island City, and the parish will record all three offices, its pastor states. The parish's house system, installed in 1911, has recorded Holy Week every year since.

columns.headline: Mr. Venn to enter the Astoria works at 9 a.m. Thursday with both instruments
columns.body: Mr. Aldous Venn of the Public Service Commission will enter the Astoria works at 9 a.m. on Thursday carrying Dr. Emil Rastin's meter and the company's, the Commission states. Alderman Feeney has asked to wait at the gate with the terrier Duke. The Commission has no objection.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: A house system was fitted at 4 p.m. in Senator Harlan's committee room at Albany for Wednesday's hearing, the Senate Clerk states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 56. Spy Wednesday tomorrow. The Speaker spies every day.

lead.headline: Wales gets the breath again, and bar twenty-three won't take the call
lead.deck: Rockaway's operator heard it; two professors in the booth heard it; four seconds of breathing reach Aberystwyth; the cable company swears the line was clear
lead.body: Dr. Strand stood in the Rockaway cable booth at two yesterday with two colleagues and the operator, sang the twenty-third bar of the WORS carol, alone this time, and the three of them heard him do it. At twenty to nine Wales cabled back. They got his hello, his goodbye and four seconds of a man breathing. The cable company says the line was clear. Rockaway's own record of the call has gone to Mr. Pike, who has not played it, or has, and is not saying.

columns.headline: Harlan puts the ears back in his room, and the Act will hear itself out
columns.body: Senator Harlan, who had the house system taken out of his committee room, had one put back in yesterday afternoon for tomorrow's hearing. The Senate Clerk says it is customary. The Senator says it is temporary. The room has not been asked.

columns.headline: Duke gets as far as the gate, and the Commission tosses him a line
columns.body: Mr. Venn goes into the Astoria works on Thursday at nine with two meters. Duke of 31st Street may not go in, but may wait at the gate with the Alderman. The Commission has no objection to gates. Duke has objections to most things, but is keeping them to himself.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: Kew Gardens buys its Easter hat over the wire
columns.body: Darlings, a Kew Gardens matron has ordered her Easter hat from Fifth Avenue by telephone, the milliner describing it down the line for eleven minutes. She will see it for the first time on Sunday morning, as will everyone else. She says it sounded divine.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The ships at Dunedin are listening for the camp now too. Nothing on the wave but the ice. The ice is not news.

lead.headline: Senate Judiciary Committee hears the Listening Act at 2 p.m. in Room 412
lead.deck: Three amendments: bedrooms, insurance adjusters, places of confession; Mr. Tully allowed one hour; a house system fitted in the room yesterday; adjournment expected April 5
lead.body: Senator Edmund Harlan's Judiciary Committee will hear the Listening Act, passed by the Assembly on March 5, at 2 p.m. today in Room 412 of the Capitol, a house system having been fitted there yesterday. Assemblyman Thomas Burkhardt speaks first. The committee will take amendments from Senator Rufus Keel on records of bedrooms, Senator Ames Whitlock on insurance adjusters, and Senator Daniel Fogarty, at the Chancery's request, on places of confession. Mr. Ambrose Tully has one hour. The Legislature expects to adjourn on April 5.

columns.headline: Ohio crest reaches New Madrid at 41.9 feet; levee 'holding'
columns.body: The Ohio's crest reached New Madrid, Missouri, at 6 p.m. yesterday, the levee station reporting the Mississippi at 41.9 feet and 'holding,' with 900 men on the bank. The station states that its house system heard 'no movement beneath' after 9 p.m.

columns.headline: Mrs. Corrigan and Mr. Gant to dance a practice hour at the Arena Saturday
columns.body: Mrs. Margaret Corrigan of Hollis and her partner, Mr. Leo Gant of Woodhaven, trombonist, will dance a practice hour at the Jamaica Arena on Saturday at 3 p.m., the management states. The marathon opens April 6 with 51 couples. Mr. Gant will not play during it.

columns.headline: Night tone calls fall to 512; Queens Light & Power 'notes the improvement'
columns.body: The Queens Exchange logged 512 calls concerning a night tone between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. yesterday, against 702 a week earlier, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. Queens Light & Power stated that it 'notes the improvement' and that the ground 'is now largely settled.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Little America has not been heard for 13 nights; the Navy states that it is 'not concerned.'

speaker.ear: Cloudy. High 52. Albany heard the Act today. Albany heard a bit more than that.

lead.headline: Harlan's new house system speaks up, and Albany resents it
lead.deck: Four hours on the Act in Room 412; bedroom, insurance and priest's clauses all go in; at twelve past five the room's own record takes down a word nobody in the room will own
lead.body: For four hours this afternoon Senator Harlan's committee heard the Listening Act in a room that, until yesterday, had no ears. Mr. Burkhardt spoke, Mr. Tully spoke for an hour against bedrooms, and the committee put in all three amendments: Keel's for the bedroom, Whitlock's for the insurance man, Fogarty's for the priest. At twelve past five the new house system took down one word, and every man in the room says it was not him. The word was 'resent.' The Senator is having the system taken out again.

columns.headline: The Ohio's crest calls at New Madrid, and the levee won't hang up
columns.body: The crest came down to New Madrid last night at forty-one feet nine, and nine hundred men sat on the levee to meet it. The levee station heard nothing moving under the bank after nine. The river is now somebody else's problem, and the levee is going to bed.

columns.headline: Night calls fall off, and the light company takes the credit on the line
columns.body: Five hundred and twelve calls about the night tone on Monday, down from seven hundred, and Queens Light & Power notes the improvement and says the ground is settled. Mr. Venn goes into the works tomorrow at nine. The company would like it known the Hum was always the ground's idea.

columns.headline: Mrs. Corrigan rehearses Saturday, and the trombone is muted for the duration
columns.body: Mrs. Corrigan and Mr. Gant will dance a practice hour at the Arena on Saturday at three. Mr. Gant, a trombonist, has promised not to play during the marathon itself, the management having heard what a trombone can do to a couple's concentration at the fortieth hour.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Thirteen nights and not a word from Byrd's camp. The Navy is not concerned. The Navy is sleeping badly.

lead.headline: Senate committee adopts the bedroom, insurance and confession amendments
lead.deck: Hearing from 2:04 p.m. to 6:10 p.m.; the word 'resent' recorded by the room's system at 5:12 p.m.; no person present identified as the speaker; the system removed at 7 p.m.; vote Monday
lead.body: Senator Edmund Harlan's Judiciary Committee heard the Listening Act from 2:04 p.m. to 6:10 p.m. yesterday and adopted the Keel amendment on records of bedrooms, 5 to 2, the Whitlock amendment licensing insurance adjusters' acoustic work, 6 to 1, and the Fogarty amendment exempting places of confession, by voice. The room's house system recorded at 5:12 p.m. the word 'resent'; no person present has been identified as the speaker. The system was removed at 7 p.m.

columns.headline: Mr. Venn enters the Astoria works at 9 a.m. today; readings to be sealed
columns.body: Mr. Aldous Venn of the Public Service Commission enters the Astoria works at 9 a.m. today with Dr. Emil Rastin's meter and the company's own. Each will be read aloud by the other side, and the readings recorded and sealed until the hearing of April 2.

columns.headline: Tenebrae sung at St. Mary's; fifteen candles extinguished in 46 minutes
columns.body: Tenebrae was sung at St. Mary's, Long Island City, at 7:30 p.m. yesterday, the fifteen candles of the hearse extinguished in 46 minutes. The noise made at the end of the office was taken down by the parish's system 'at unusual length,' the pastor states.

columns.headline: Valves at 80 cents the sleeve; eggs at 54 for Easter
columns.body: The sleeve of receiving valves sold at 80 cents at the Vantry Arcade's hardware counter yesterday, Mr. Fass reports, and eggs at 54 cents. Mr. Fass states that it is 'the first week since 1926 that a sleeve has cost less than a dozen and a half of eggs.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Mississippi at New Madrid fell to 41.4 feet at midnight; the levee station reports 'quiet.'

speaker.ear: Fair. High 58. Maundy Thursday. Mr. Venn went in. We waited outside with the dog.

lead.headline: Venn goes in with two meters, and Duke holds the line at the gate
lead.deck: Six hours and ten minutes inside the Astoria works; each side reads the other's meter aloud; the readings sealed in wax till Tuesday; the Alderman and his terrier keep watch on the pavement
lead.body: At nine this morning Mr. Venn of the Commission walked into the Astoria works of Queens Light & Power with a meter under each arm, Dr. Rastin's and the company's, and walked out at ten past three with neither, both being locked in the Commission's van with the sealed readings. Nobody will say what either meter read. Alderman Feeney stood at the gate all day with Duke of 31st Street, who lay down facing the works at nine and did not move until Mr. Venn came out. Then Duke barked, once.

columns.headline: Albany's new house system hears one word, and the Senator pulls the plug
columns.body: Room 412 had ears for one day. At twelve past five yesterday they heard 'resent,' nobody in the room owned it, and by seven the Senator had the system pulled out of the wall. The committee votes on Monday. The wall has not been asked how it feels.

columns.headline: St. Mary's puts the candles out one by one, and the record keeps the last word
columns.body: Fifteen candles out in forty-six minutes at Tenebrae last night, and then the clatter of books on pews that ends it, which St. Mary's record took down, says the pastor, at unusual length. He is not complaining. He says it was a very devout clatter.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Can you hold my Easter eggs?'
columns.body: Madam, the operator cannot hold eggs. She can hold a line, and does, eleven hours a day. Eggs are fifty-four cents this week and valves eighty, so if you want something that will keep until Sunday, the operator suggests the valves.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Duke barked once when Mr. Venn came out. The Commission has asked that the bark be entered in the record. It already was.

lead.headline: Commission engineer six hours ten minutes in the Astoria works; readings sealed
lead.deck: Mr. Venn entered at 9 a.m. and left at 3:10 p.m.; both instruments read aloud by the opposing parties and recorded; Mr. Tisch: the company's meter 'read as it always reads'
lead.body: Mr. Aldous Venn of the Public Service Commission spent six hours ten minutes in the Astoria works of Queens Light & Power yesterday, entering at 9 a.m. with Dr. Emil Rastin's meter and the company's, and leaving at 3:10 p.m. The readings of both instruments were read aloud by the opposing representatives, recorded, and sealed in the Commission's presence. Mr. Roland Tisch, for the company, stated that its meter 'read as it always reads.' Dr. Rastin declined to comment before Tuesday's hearing.

columns.headline: Three Hours' Agony in 34 Queens churches; Exchange asks for quiet lines
columns.body: The Three Hours' Agony will be observed from noon to 3 p.m. today in 34 Queens churches and carried by telephone from nine parishes, the Chancery states. The Queens Exchange asks subscribers to place no calls between noon and 3 p.m. 'except in sickness or fire.'

columns.headline: Corona grocers asked for their sardine sales since November
columns.body: Detective Sergeant Edward Moran stated yesterday that the three Corona grocers who sell the Portland sardine found in Mr. Joseph Marchetti's tool bag have been asked for their records of sales since November. The bench warrant for Mr. Marchetti remains outstanding.

columns.headline: No decision on the Riverhead seal expected before April 15, clerk states
columns.body: The clerk of the Appellate Division states that no decision on Mr. Francis Gorman's appeal against the Board of Elections' seal on 11 seconds of its Riverhead record is expected before April 15. Mr. Gorman stated that he 'can wait 11 seconds longer.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Venn's sealed readings were delivered to the Commission's Albany office at 11:20 p.m.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 55. Good Friday. The Speaker kept it down from noon to three.

lead.headline: A tin comes back on the line, but Party Line says it's a wrong number
lead.deck: Good Friday's parcel post brings sardines to Position 43 for the first time since February; the postmark is Jamaica, the string is kitchen string, and the cat walks away
lead.body: At ten past four, for the first time in five Fridays, the parcel post brought a tin of sardines to the Queens Exchange addressed to Party Line. The operators cheered. Then they looked. The postmark was Jamaica, not Corona. The string was kitchen string, not lineman's cord. The sardines were Norwegian, not Portland. Party Line sniffed it once, walked to the warm end of the board, and sat down where the Corona calls come in. Sergeant Moran has the tin. He says it is a common make.

columns.headline: Venn's readings go to Albany sealed, and the company's meter stays on message
columns.body: Mr. Venn's readings of both meters went to the Commission's Albany office in wax last night. Mr. Tisch says the company's meter read as it always reads. Dr. Rastin says nothing until Tuesday. Duke, asked, lay down facing Albany, the first time he has faced anything but Astoria.

columns.headline: The Exchange goes quiet from noon to three, and the whole borough holds
columns.body: From noon to three today the Exchange asked Queens to ring nobody except for sickness or fire, and Queens obliged. Ninety-one calls came through for sickness and two for fire. One woman rang at half past two to say she had kept quiet, and wanted somebody to know.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Pike plays the Rockaway record, and keeps the result off the air
columns.body: Mr. Pike has played the Rockaway cable station's record of Dr. Strand singing the twenty-third bar to Wales. He will not say whether the bar is on it. He has asked Dr. Strand to come in on Tuesday. WORS itself has been silent eighteen nights.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Party Line has not touched the Jamaica tin. The operators are eating it. It is very good.

record.ear: Fair and warmer. High 60. Low 45. Holy Saturday.

lead.headline: Little America heard after fifteen nights; message concerns the dogs
lead.deck: Forty words received at Bay Shore; the camp 'all well, 47 below'; eleven pups born in the fortnight; 'the dogs will not stop singing'; no reason given for the silence
lead.body: The Navy's receiving station at Bay Shore heard Little America at 10:12 p.m. yesterday, for the first time since March 14, a message of 40 words from Commander Byrd's camp. The message states that the camp is 'all well, 47 below,' that eleven pups were born to the sledge dogs 'in the past fortnight,' and that 'the dogs will not stop singing.' It gives no reason for the silence. The message was played in the Record's window at 11 p.m. to about 300.

columns.headline: Week's count: 2,830 night calls on the tone; 1,104 of them on Thursday night
columns.body: The Queens Exchange logged 2,830 calls concerning a night tone between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday, Superintendent Arne states, against 4,870 the week before. Of these, 1,104 came on the night following Mr. Venn's inspection of the Astoria works.

columns.headline: Holy Saturday offices at St. Mary's from 6:30 a.m.; new fire at the door
columns.body: The Holy Saturday offices will begin at 6:30 a.m. today at St. Mary's, Long Island City, with the blessing of the new fire at the church door, the pastor states, and the Exsultet will be sung at about 7:15. The parish will record the offices in full.

columns.headline: Sand laid beneath the elevated eight mornings running; no horse down
columns.body: Transit Commission crews have sanded Roosevelt Avenue beneath the elevated by 5 a.m. on eight mornings running, and no horse has fallen there since the order, Mr. Dennis Rafferty of the carters' association states. The association's man has walked the avenue each morning 'and found the sand.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The child of 61st Street, Woodside, said goodnight to the family set at 7:40 p.m. yesterday and was not answered, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 60. Holy Saturday. Hats are being finished all over Queens.

lead.headline: Byrd's camp comes back on the air, and the dogs get the last word
lead.deck: Fifteen nights of dead air, then forty words from the bottom of the world: all well, forty-seven below, eleven pups, and the dogs will not stop singing
lead.body: For fifteen nights the Navy's men at Bay Shore heard nothing from Little America, and at twelve past ten last night the camp came through with forty words, as though it had only stepped out to the shop. All well. Forty-seven below. Eleven pups born in the fortnight. And the dogs will not stop singing. That was the message. Not a word about why the camp went quiet. Three hundred people heard it in the Record's window and cheered the pups. We cheer them too.

columns.headline: Week's count: the Hum's calls drop by half, then pick up the night Venn leaves
columns.body: Two thousand eight hundred and thirty calls about the tone this week, down from four thousand eight hundred and seventy. Eleven hundred and four came on Thursday night, after Mr. Venn had been through the works. The light company says that was the thaw. The thaw was a month ago.

columns.headline: Mrs. Corrigan steps out with the band, and the Arena gives her a fine reception
columns.body: Mrs. Corrigan and Mr. Gant danced their practice hour at the Jamaica Arena at three before four hundred, and did not stop. Mr. Gant kept time by humming, which the management allows. The marathon opens a week tonight. Mrs. Corrigan says she is ready. Mr. Gant's lip says nothing.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Will the Easter parade be on the wire?'
columns.body: Sir, Fifth Avenue will be carried from the Cathedral steps from eleven tomorrow, but you will hear only footsteps and the word 'darling.' The parade is a thing for seeing, and seeing costs dear. The operator advises a hat, a hatpin and a trolley fare.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Eleven pups at Little America. We have proposed eleven names. The Navy has declined all eleven.

editorial.headline: Ribbons on the locked doors
editorial.body: This week, eighteen years after the Triangle fire, every factory door in Long Island City that is locked from the outside during working hours was found tied with a black ribbon and a card bearing the name of one of the hundred and forty-six who died behind a locked door in 1911. There were more doors than names. The Fire Inspector, Mr. Elias Root, who has certified those doors open since 1924, was found tied to his own office door with ribbon of the same kind. This paper deplores vandalism. We have written to Mr. Root asking if he is well. We have not yet had an answer. We understand his door is locked.

lead.headline: The Holy Saturday offices at St. Mary's, Long Island City, as recorded
lead.deck: From 6:31 a.m. to 9:48 a.m.; the new fire struck at 6:34; the Exsultet sung in 11 minutes; the bells rung at the Gloria; the parish record printed in part
lead.body: The Holy Saturday offices at St. Mary's, Long Island City, ran from 6:31 a.m. to 9:48 a.m. yesterday. The record gives: 6:34, the new fire struck at the church door; 6:51, 'Lumen Christi,' three times, each higher; 7:14 to 7:25, the Exsultet; 8:02, the bells, silent since Thursday, rung at the Gloria; 9:48, the doors. Between 7:25 and 7:26 the record holds a low tone the pastor 'did not hear in the church.'

columns.headline: Little America's message played four times in the Record's window
columns.body: Commander Byrd's message of Friday night from Little America, with its report of eleven pups and that 'the dogs will not stop singing,' was played four times in the Record's window to about 1,100. The camp was heard again at 10:30 p.m.: 'All well.'

columns.headline: Easter promenade to be carried from the Cathedral steps from 11 a.m.
columns.body: The Easter promenade on Fifth Avenue will be carried by wire from the steps of St. Patrick's Cathedral from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. today. The Weather Bureau forecasts fair and 62. Police expect about 200,000 on the avenue between 49th and 57th Streets.

columns.headline: Week ahead: Senate committee votes Monday; Greenpoint heard Tuesday
columns.body: Senator Edmund Harlan's Judiciary Committee votes on the amended Listening Act at Albany on Monday. The Public Service Commission hears the Greenpoint petitioners on Tuesday, when Mr. Aldous Venn's sealed readings of March 28 will be opened. The Jamaica marathon opens on Saturday at 8 p.m.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Bells were rung at midnight in 23 Queens parishes; the Exchange received 14 calls asking which.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 62. Easter Sunday. Hats on, Queens.

lead.headline: The Easter hats go out on the wire, and Kew Gardens finally hears its own
lead.deck: Two hundred thousand on the avenue, two hours on the line, and not a feather audible; our man counts 312 plumes, 40 fruit bowls and one birdcage; the telephone hat makes its debut
lead.body: From eleven to one today the wire from the Cathedral steps carried Fifth Avenue's Easter promenade into Queens, and Queens heard two hundred thousand pairs of shoes, a great many people saying 'darling,' and a man selling lilies. Hats cannot be heard. The Speaker sent a man anyway. He counts three hundred and twelve hats with feathers, forty with fruit, one with a small birdcage, and one from Kew Gardens, ordered by telephone and never seen till today. Its owner says it looks exactly as it sounded.

columns.headline: Easter bells ring at midnight, and the Exchange gets fourteen wrong numbers
columns.body: Twenty-three Queens parishes rang their bells at midnight, and fourteen people rang the Exchange to ask which one they had heard. The operator, who heard all twenty-three at once through the board, told each caller it was theirs. It is Easter. Everybody gets a bell.

columns.headline: St. Mary's plays back the Vigil, and finds one note more than the choir sang
columns.body: St. Mary's record of the offices runs three hours and seventeen minutes, and after the Exsultet there is a minute of a low tone the pastor says nobody in the church heard. He played it to the choir. The choir says it was not them. The organist has an alibi.

columns.headline: Byrd's dogs are a hit on the wire, and Jackson Avenue wants an encore
columns.body: Eleven hundred people heard Commander Byrd's message played in the Record's window yesterday, four times, and every time it reached the dogs singing they cheered. The camp came through again last night: all well. It did not mention the dogs. We think they had been told to hush.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: A Sunnyside reader writes that her Easter ham was louder than her hat. We print this without comment, as we print everything.
